---
title: "Monotonic Queue"
description: "From children passing a window to the sliding-window maximum: a deque kept in decreasing order, why its front is the window maximum, why each index enters and leaves once, two deques for max and min, the deque inside a dynamic program, and hard interview problems solved math-first."
---

A monotonic queue answers "what is the largest value in the last $k$ items?" every time a new item arrives, in $O(1)$ amortized time. It is a double-ended queue (a *deque*) with one house rule: its values always decrease from front to back. This lesson builds it from the slow window scan, proves that each index enters and leaves at most once, and then uses it for moving windows, two-pointer windows and a dynamic program.

All code is in [`MonotonicQueueLab.java`](MonotonicQueueLab.java). Run it from this folder with `java MonotonicQueueLab.java`; it checks every number on this page and prints `OK`.

## The problem

Six readings arrive one by one: `a = [2, 7, 3, 1, 5, 4]` (positions 0 to 5). After each reading we want the **maximum of the last $k = 3$ readings**:

| Window (positions) | Values | Maximum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 to 2 | 2, 7, 3 | 7 |
| 1 to 3 | 7, 3, 1 | 7 |
| 2 to 4 | 3, 1, 5 | 5 |
| 3 to 5 | 1, 5, 4 | 5 |

- The obvious method rescans each window: $k - 1$ comparisons for each of the $n - k + 1$ windows. Here that is $4 \times 2 = 8$, but for $n = 100{,}000$ and $k = 50{,}000$ it is about $2.5 \times 10^9$.
- A heap would give $O(n \log n)$. We want $O(n)$: each reading handled a constant number of times, at most $2n = 12$ deque operations here.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip}
You stand at a window that is three children wide, and children walk past it in a line, one step at a time. After every step you must shout the name of the **tallest child you can see**.

You keep a short list of children who *might still* be the tallest. When a new child appears at the window, look at the end of your list. Anyone there who is not taller than the newcomer is **crossed off for ever**. They will walk out of the window before the newcomer does, and while both are visible the newcomer is at least as tall. They can never win again.

So your list is always sorted, tallest first. The answer is simply the first name on it. When that child walks out of the window, cross them off the front.

Each child is written on the list once and crossed off at most once, so for six children you write and cross out at most $2 \times 6 = 12$ times, however tall they are.

Antti Laaksonen's free *Competitive Programmer's Handbook* (§8.3, "Sliding window minimum") teaches the same trick for the minimum, with the same "added once, removed at most once" argument.
:::

## From simple to advanced

### Level 1: rescan every window

Write the definition straight down. The window that ends at position $i$ is positions $i - k + 1$ to $i$:

$$
M_i = \max \lbrace a_t : i - k + 1 \le t \le i \rbrace, \qquad i = k - 1, \dots, n - 1
$$

where:

- $a_t$ is the reading at position $t$;
- $k$ is the window length and $n$ the number of readings;
- $M_i$ is the maximum of the window that **ends** at $i$, defined once a full window exists ($i \ge k - 1$).

Example: $M_4 = \max \lbrace a_2, a_3, a_4 \rbrace = \max \lbrace 3, 1, 5 \rbrace = 5$.

```java
static int[] windowMaxBrute(int[] a, int k) {
    int[] result = new int[a.length - k + 1];
    for (int start = 0; start + k <= a.length; start++) {
        int max = a[start];
        for (int i = start + 1; i < start + k; i++) max = Math.max(max, a[i]);
        result[start] = max;
    }
    return result;
}
```

It costs $(n - k + 1)(k - 1)$ comparisons, which is $O(n k)$.

### Level 2: throw away readings that can never win

The key observation is **domination**. Take two positions $s < t$ inside the same window:

$$
s < t \;\land\; a_s \le a_t \implies a_s \text{ is never again the maximum of any window that contains it}
$$

where:

- $\land$ means "and" and $\implies$ means "therefore";
- $s$ is the older reading and $t$ the newer one;
- every future window that still contains $s$ also contains $t$, because $s$ leaves first, and $a_t \ge a_s$.

Example: in `a = [2, 7, 3, 1, 5, 4]`, reading $a_4 = 5$ dominates $a_2 = 3$ and $a_3 = 1$. Windows 2 to 4 and 3 to 5 both contain position 4, so neither 3 nor 1 can ever be their maximum.

So keep only the **undominated** positions in a deque $q_1, q_2, \dots, q_m$ from front to back. They satisfy

$$
q_1 < q_2 < \dots < q_m \quad\text{and}\quad a_{q_1} > a_{q_2} > \dots > a_{q_m}
$$

where:

- $q_1$ is the front (oldest survivor) and $q_m$ the back (newest);
- positions increase from front to back, because we always add at the back;
- values strictly decrease, because a newcomer pops every value $\le$ itself from the back before joining.

Therefore the front $a_{q_1}$ is the largest value in the deque, and the window maximum. Each step does three things: drop the front if it has left the window, pop dominated values from the back, and push the newcomer.

Example: the trace on `a = [2, 7, 3, 1, 5, 4]` with $k = 3$. The deque column lists positions with their values in brackets.

| $i$ | $a_i$ | Front expired? | Popped from back | Deque after | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 | — | — | 0 (2) | — |
| 1 | 7 | — | 0 | 1 (7) | — |
| 2 | 3 | — | — | 1 (7), 2 (3) | 7 |
| 3 | 1 | — | — | 1 (7), 2 (3), 3 (1) | 7 |
| 4 | 5 | 1, since $1 \le 4 - 3$ | 3, then 2 | 4 (5) | 5 |
| 5 | 4 | — | — | 4 (5), 5 (4) | 5 |

The output is `[7, 7, 5, 5]`, the table in "The problem".

```java
static int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    int[] result = new int[a.length - k + 1];
    Deque<Integer> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (!deque.isEmpty() && deque.peekFirst() <= i - k) deque.pollFirst();       // front left the window
        while (!deque.isEmpty() && a[deque.peekLast()] <= a[i]) deque.pollLast();   // dominated by a[i]
        deque.addLast(i);
        if (i >= k - 1) result[i - k + 1] = a[deque.peekFirst()];
    }
    return result;
}
```

Store **positions**, not values: a position tells you both the value (`a[q]`) and whether it has left the window (`q <= i - k`). At most one position expires per step, because the window moves by one, so an `if` is enough at the front.

### Level 3: counting the work, at most $2n$ operations

The `while` loop can pop several positions at once (at $i = 4$ it popped two), but over the whole run

$$
\text{adds} + \text{pops} \le n + n = 2n
$$

where:

- $n$ is the number of readings;
- every position is added at the back **exactly once**, so there are $n$ adds;
- every position leaves at most once, either from the back (dominated) or from the front (expired), so there are at most $n$ pops in total.

Example: for our six readings there are 6 adds, 3 back pops (positions 0, 3 and 2) and 1 front pop (position 1): $6 + 3 + 1 = 10 \le 12$. Compare 8 comparisons for the brute force here; the deque wins as soon as $k$ grows, because its cost does not depend on $k$ at all.

**The minimum** works the same way with the comparison flipped: pop from the back while `a[back] >= a[i]`, and the deque increases from front to back.

**Ties.** Popping on `<=` keeps only the newest of equal values, which is the one that stays longest. Popping on `<` keeps all of them; that is also correct, just a little longer.

### Level 4: the deque inside a dynamic program

Many dynamic programs take the best of the last $k$ answers:

$$
f_i = c_i + \max_{i - k \le j < i} f_j, \qquad f_0 = c_0
$$

where:

- $c_i$ is the score of step $i$;
- $f_i$ is the best total score of a path that ends at step $i$;
- the path may jump forward at most $k$ steps, so step $i$ can be reached from any $j$ in $[i - k, i - 1]$.

That $\max$ is a sliding-window maximum over the values $f_j$ already computed, so a deque replaces an $O(k)$ scan. This is LeetCode 1696 (Jump Game VI).

Example: $c = [1, -1, -2, 4, -7, 3]$ and $k = 2$.

- $f_0 = 1$.
- $f_1 = -1 + \max(f_0) = -1 + 1 = 0$.
- $f_2 = -2 + \max(f_0, f_1) = -2 + 1 = -1$.
- $f_3 = 4 + \max(f_1, f_2) = 4 + 0 = 4$.
- $f_4 = -7 + \max(f_2, f_3) = -7 + 4 = -3$.
- $f_5 = 3 + \max(f_3, f_4) = 3 + 4 = 7$.

The best path scores **7**: steps $0 \to 1 \to 3 \to 5$, which is $1 - 1 + 4 + 3 = 7$.

```java
static int maxJumpScore(int[] nums, int k) {
    int[] best = new int[nums.length];                 // best[i] = top score of a path that ends on i
    Deque<Integer> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();         // indices; best[] decreases from front to back
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (!deque.isEmpty() && deque.peekFirst() < i - k) deque.pollFirst();
        best[i] = nums[i] + (deque.isEmpty() ? 0 : best[deque.peekFirst()]);
        while (!deque.isEmpty() && best[deque.peekLast()] <= best[i]) deque.pollLast();
        deque.addLast(i);
    }
    return best[nums.length - 1];
}
```

The order inside the loop matters: read the front **before** adding $i$, because $f_i$ must use only earlier steps. The time drops from $O(n k)$ to $O(n)$.

## Why it works and what it costs

**The invariant.** *After step $i$, the deque holds, in increasing order of position, exactly those positions $t$ in the current window with $a_t > a_u$ for every later position $u$ in the window, so their values strictly decrease.*

- *Initially* the deque is empty and no window exists, so it holds.
- *Step $i$ maintains it.* The front check removes the one position that left the window. The `while` loop removes every position whose value is $\le a_i$: those are dominated by $i$ and, by the rule in Level 2, can never be a maximum again. Every position that stays has a value $> a_i$, and $i$ joins at the back.
- *Therefore the front is the maximum.* Any window position missing from the deque was dominated by a later position $t$ with a value at least as large. Either $t$ is in the deque, or it was dominated in turn by an even later one, and so on. That chain ends at a deque member with a value at least as large, and the front is the largest deque member.

**Costs**, for $n$ readings and window length $k$:

| Method | Time | Extra space | Operations for $n = 6$, $k = 3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Level 1, rescan every window | $O(n k)$ | $O(1)$ | 8 comparisons |
| Max-heap with lazy deletion | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n)$ | — |
| Level 2, monotonic deque | $O(n)$ | $O(k)$ deque | 10 adds and pops, $\le 2n = 12$ |

The deque never holds more than $k$ positions, because everything in it is inside the window.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Storing values instead of positions | You cannot tell when the front has left the window | Store indices, and expire when `index <= i - k` |
| Off by one in the expiry test | Windows of size $k + 1$, wrong maxima | The window ending at `i` starts at `i - k + 1`, so expire positions `<= i - k`; draw it for $k = 3$ |
| Reading the front before expiring it | A maximum from outside the window | Expire first, then pop dominated values, then push, then read |
| Popping from the front for domination | The deque stops being sorted | Dominated values are always at the **back**, next to the newcomer |
| In a DP, pushing $i$ before computing $f_i$ | $f_i$ uses itself | Read the front, compute $f_i$, then push $i$ |
| Calling it $O(n k)$ because of the inner `while` | Rejecting a linear solution | Each index is added once and removed once: at most $2n$ operations |

## Interview problems

Each solution starts with the mathematics. Once the formula is right, the code is short.

### 1. LeetCode 1438: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit (Medium)

**Problem.** Return the length of the longest subarray in which every two elements differ by at most `limit`. For `nums = [8, 2, 4, 7]` and `limit = 4` the answer is 2, from `[2, 4]` or `[4, 7]`.

**Math first.** Every pair is within the limit exactly when the extreme pair is:

$$
\max_{l \le t \le r} a_t - \min_{l \le t \le r} a_t \le \text{limit}
$$

where:

- $[l, r]$ is the subarray from position $l$ to position $r$;
- the largest difference of any pair is the maximum minus the minimum, so one test covers all pairs.

If $[l, r]$ is valid, so is every shorter window $[l', r]$ with $l' \ge l$, because removing elements cannot widen the spread. So two pointers work: move $r$ forward, and move $l$ forward only while the window is invalid. One decreasing deque gives the maximum and one increasing deque gives the minimum.

Example: `[8, 2, 4, 7]`, limit 4.

- $r = 0$: window `[8]`, spread $0$, length 1.
- $r = 1$: `[8, 2]` has spread $8 - 2 = 6 > 4$, so $l$ moves to 1: `[2]`, length 1.
- $r = 2$: `[2, 4]`, spread $2 \le 4$, length **2**.
- $r = 3$: `[2, 4, 7]` has spread $7 - 2 = 5 > 4$, so $l$ moves to 2: `[4, 7]`, spread 3, length 2.

The best length is 2.

**Idea.** Keep `maxQ` decreasing and `minQ` increasing, both holding positions. After adding $r$, while the fronts differ by more than the limit, advance `left` and drop any front that fell out.

```java
static int longestSubarray(int[] nums, int limit) {
    Deque<Integer> maxQ = new ArrayDeque<>(), minQ = new ArrayDeque<>();   // indices
    int left = 0, best = 0;
    for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        while (!maxQ.isEmpty() && nums[maxQ.peekLast()] <= nums[right]) maxQ.pollLast();
        while (!minQ.isEmpty() && nums[minQ.peekLast()] >= nums[right]) minQ.pollLast();
        maxQ.addLast(right);
        minQ.addLast(right);
        while (nums[maxQ.peekFirst()] - nums[minQ.peekFirst()] > limit) {
            left++;                                    // shrink from the left until max - min <= limit
            if (maxQ.peekFirst() < left) maxQ.pollFirst();
            if (minQ.peekFirst() < left) minQ.pollFirst();
        }
        best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
```

**Answer.** 2 for the example, 4 for `[10, 1, 2, 4, 7, 2]` with limit 5 (the subarray `[2, 4, 7, 2]`), and 3 for `[4, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 2, 2]` with limit 0. Each pointer moves at most $n$ times and each deque does at most $2n$ operations, so the time is $O(n)$ and the space $O(n)$. For $n = 10^5$ that is a few hundred thousand steps, against about $5 \times 10^9$ subarrays for a brute force.

### 2. LeetCode 239: Sliding Window Maximum (Hard)

**Problem.** Return the maximum of every window of length $k$. For `nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]` and $k = 3$ the answer is `[3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]`.

**Math first.** We need $M_i$ for every $i \ge k - 1$, and the deque from Level 2 keeps

$$
M_i = a_{q_1}, \qquad a_{q_1} > a_{q_2} > \dots > a_{q_m}, \qquad i - k < q_1
$$

where:

- $M_i$ is the maximum of the window ending at $i$;
- $q_1, \dots, q_m$ are the deque positions from front to back;
- $i - k < q_1$ says the front is still inside the window.

Example: at $i = 4$ the window is `[-1, -3, 5]` (positions 2 to 4). Before step 4 the deque holds positions 1, 2, 3 with values $3 > -1 > -3$. Position 1 expires because $1 \le 4 - 3$. The newcomer $a_4 = 5$ pops $-3$ and $-1$. The deque is just position 4, so $M_4 = 5$.

**Idea.** This is Level 2 unchanged: expire the front, pop dominated values from the back, push $i$, and read the front once the first window is full.

```java
static int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    int[] result = new int[a.length - k + 1];
    Deque<Integer> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (!deque.isEmpty() && deque.peekFirst() <= i - k) deque.pollFirst();       // front left the window
        while (!deque.isEmpty() && a[deque.peekLast()] <= a[i]) deque.pollLast();   // dominated by a[i]
        deque.addLast(i);
        if (i >= k - 1) result[i - k + 1] = a[deque.peekFirst()];
    }
    return result;
}
```

**Answer.** `[3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]`, and `[1]` for `nums = [1]`, $k = 1$. The fronts at $i = 2, \dots, 7$ are the values $3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7$. $O(n)$ time and $O(k)$ space. For the limits $n = 10^5$ and $k$ up to $10^5$ that is at most $2 \times 10^5$ deque operations, while rescanning could need billions of comparisons.

### 3. LeetCode 1499: Max Value of Equation (Hard)

**Problem.** Points $(x_i, y_i)$ are sorted by strictly increasing $x$. Over all pairs $i < j$ with $x_j - x_i \le k$, return the maximum of $y_i + y_j + \lvert x_i - x_j \rvert$. For `points = [[1, 3], [2, 0], [5, 10], [6, -10]]` and $k = 1$ the answer is 4.

**Math first.** Because $x_i < x_j$, the absolute value opens as $x_j - x_i$, and the expression **splits** into a part for $j$ and a part for $i$:

$$
y_i + y_j + (x_j - x_i) = \underbrace{(y_j + x_j)}_{\text{fixed for } j} + \underbrace{(y_i - x_i)}_{\text{best earlier } i}, \qquad x_j - x_i \le k
$$

where:

- $j$ is the current point and $i$ any earlier point;
- $y_j + x_j$ does not depend on $i$, so for a fixed $j$ we only need the largest $y_i - x_i$;
- the condition $x_j - x_i \le k$ is a window over $x$: points too far to the left drop out for ever.

So the problem is a sliding-window maximum of $y_i - x_i$, with a window measured in $x$ instead of in positions.

Example: $k = 1$.

- $j = 1$, point $(2, 0)$: point 0 has $x_1 - x_0 = 2 - 1 = 1 \le 1$ and $y_0 - x_0 = 3 - 1 = 2$. The value is $(0 + 2) + 2 = 4$.
- $j = 2$, point $(5, 10)$: points 0 and 1 are too far ($5 - 2 = 3 > 1$), so there is no pair.
- $j = 3$, point $(6, -10)$: point 2 has $6 - 5 = 1 \le 1$ and $10 - 5 = 5$. The value is $(-10 + 6) + 5 = 1$.

The maximum is $\max(4, 1) = 4$.

**Idea.** Keep a deque of earlier points whose $y - x$ strictly decreases from front to back. For each new point: drop fronts that are more than $k$ away, use the front to score the pair, then pop dominated points from the back and add the new one.

```java
static int findMaxValueOfEquation(int[][] points, int k) {
    Deque<int[]> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();           // pairs {x, y - x}; y - x decreases from front to back
    int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    for (int[] p : points) {
        int x = p[0], y = p[1];
        while (!deque.isEmpty() && x - deque.peekFirst()[0] > k) deque.pollFirst();
        if (!deque.isEmpty()) best = Math.max(best, x + y + deque.peekFirst()[1]);
        while (!deque.isEmpty() && deque.peekLast()[1] <= y - x) deque.pollLast();
        deque.addLast(new int[] {x, y - x});
    }
    return best;
}
```

The front check is a `while`, not an `if`: the window is measured in $x$, so one step can push several old points out at once (at $j = 2$ both points 0 and 1 leave).

**Answer.** 4 for the example, and 3 for `[[0, 0], [3, 0], [9, 2]]` with $k = 3$. Each point enters and leaves the deque once: $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space. Checking all pairs would cost $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, which is about $5 \times 10^9$ for $n = 10^5$.

## Mathematical Abstraction

A monotonic queue maintains the maximum of a sliding window by keeping only the undominated positions, in order:

$$
M_i = \max_{i - k < t \le i} a_t = a_{q_1}, \qquad q_1 < q_2 < \dots < q_m, \qquad a_{q_1} > a_{q_2} > \dots > a_{q_m}
$$

where:

- $a$ is the sequence, $k$ the window length and $M_i$ the maximum of the window ending at $i$;
- $q_1, \dots, q_m$ are the positions in the deque, front to back, all inside the window;
- a position is removed from the back when a newer value is at least as large, and from the front when it leaves the window, so each position is added once and removed at most once: at most $2n$ operations.

Example: for `a = [2, 7, 3, 1, 5, 4]` and $k = 3$, at $i = 5$ the deque is positions 4, 5 with values $5 > 4$, so $M_5 = a_4 = 5$. The whole run makes 6 adds and 4 removals, $10 \le 12$. Splitting a two-index objective into "part for $j$" plus "part for $i$" (LeetCode 1499) or taking the best of the last $k$ DP values (LeetCode 1696) turns other problems into this same window maximum.
